title: Polynomial-time chemical accuracy for molecular electronic structure

concept.text: The innovation would be a proved algorithm that calculates molecular ground-state electronic energies to a specified chemical-accuracy tolerance with total computational cost bounded by a polynomial. It would exploit the structure of a clearly defined family of molecular Coulomb Hamiltonians under the Born–Oppenheimer approximation, in which the nuclei are held fixed while the electronic problem is solved. The algorithm could be classical or quantum. The target is a reliable energy calculation for difficult molecules, with both its error and its computational requirements established.

The scope must identify the molecular family, the representation of the electronic Hamiltonian, the number of electrons and basis functions, the precision of the input, and the meaning of the energy-error guarantee. An accuracy guarantee for a Hamiltonian expressed in a finite basis is different from a guarantee that also includes basis truncation and other modeling errors. A method proved efficient for a restricted molecular family would establish that scope; it would not establish efficient calculation for every molecule or every local Hamiltonian.

The supplied research identifies McArdle and coauthors’ 2020 review, Quantum computational chemistry, as the technical background for the computational challenge and possible quantum approaches. The source index contains no retained copy of that review, so its specific passages and qualifications could not be checked in the supplied review. The algorithm described here remains a hypothetical target; the supplied materials do not establish that it has been achieved.

significance.text: Full configuration interaction represents the electronic state using a number of configurations that grows combinatorially when electron count and orbital count grow together. This makes general exact diagonalization increasingly difficult. Density-functional and coupled-cluster methods make many useful calculations possible, but difficult transition-metal systems and bond-breaking problems require careful assessment of the particular approximation and system. A proved, practical polynomial-cost method covering a broad family of such difficult molecules would substantially expand access to reliable first-principles energies. These technical motivations appear in the supplied research, although the cited review’s treatment could not be verified from retained source text.

Conditional impact assessment: reliable energies could become a much more accessible input to comparing molecular structures, evaluating reaction energetics, and investigating candidate catalysts and materials. The extent of that improvement would depend on the breadth of the molecular family and on practical computational costs. A polynomial with large constants or a high degree could remain unusable at chemically relevant sizes. Accuracy in energy differences would also need attention: separate guarantees on total energies must be sufficient for the differences used in a particular chemical decision.

The direct output specified by this innovation is ground-state energy. Electron density, forces, excited states, and other observables would require additional procedures with their own cost and accuracy analyses. Even reliable electronic energies would supply only part of a materials or molecular design workflow. Additional calculations, synthesis, and experimental validation would still determine whether a proposed material or molecule performs as intended.

The complexity-theory analogy has a strict boundary. The supplied research attributes to Troyer and Wiese’s 2005 paper a result connecting a general polynomial solution of the fermionic sign problem with polynomial-time solution of NP problems. Its precise assumptions could not be inspected because no source artifact was retained. Regardless of that attribution, success for a structured molecular subclass would not by itself supply a general sign-problem solver or establish P = NP. A quantum molecular algorithm would likewise not, merely by being efficient, establish a classical polynomial-time algorithm for NP-complete problems.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is an end-to-end method that combines a useful molecular scope, a rigorous energy-error guarantee, and polynomial total cost. The proof must cover all parameters that can carry computational difficulty, rather than expressing cost only in electron count while leaving basis size, input precision, requested accuracy, or other consequential parameters implicit. It must also state any promises or restrictions defining the family to which it applies.

For a quantum approach based on phase estimation, efficient simulation of the Hamiltonian is only part of the task. The method must account for preparing a state with sufficient ground-state overlap and for the repetitions or other procedures required to achieve the claimed success probability. An efficiently executed energy measurement does not establish efficient access to the ground-state energy if obtaining a suitable initial state is prohibitively expensive. The supplied research associates this issue with the McArdle review, but the review’s exact discussion is unavailable in the retained record.

Error control is a separate barrier from favorable scaling. The algorithm must distinguish numerical or quantum-estimation error from errors introduced by the finite basis and the physical model. Any claim extending beyond the specified finite-basis Hamiltonian needs corresponding control of those additional errors. Certification must itself fit within the total cost bound; relying on otherwise infeasible exact diagonalization to certify every large calculation would leave the practical target incomplete.

A classical solution would need to exploit molecular structure strongly enough to avoid the combinatorial burden of a general full-configuration representation within its claimed family. Generic sign-problem hardness does not decide whether that structured family admits such an algorithm. The supplied record therefore supports preserving the molecular target as a distinct question, while leaving its present-day resolution and any applicable complexity restrictions unsettled.

current_state.text: The historical account in the supplied research states that quantum algorithms with polynomial asymptotic scaling had been published since the 2000s and that the hardware demonstrations covered by the 2020 McArdle review involved molecules already tractable on classical computers. These are dated claims from the research, not independently verified findings of this record: the source index retains neither the review text nor an extracted passage sufficient to check their scope. In particular, a polynomial scaling claim for an algorithmic component must be distinguished from a complete ground-state calculation that includes state preparation and error control.

The supplied research describes density-functional and coupled-cluster calculations as important practical tools. Its earlier blanket characterization of these methods as uncontrolled for the hardest cases is too broad: reliability depends on the chosen method, approximation, and molecular system. Similarly, the relevant scaling statement is that full configuration interaction has combinatorial worst-case growth as electron and orbital counts increase together; this should not be expanded into an identical scaling claim for every exact classical method or every restricted molecular family.

The research also attributes to the 2020 review the view that further theoretical developments may be needed even with error-corrected quantum hardware. No retained passage is available to verify that attribution or its qualifications. Historical hardware assessments cannot establish the situation in 2026, and the continued applicability of a historical statement about an algorithmic gap requires separate evidence.

No 2024–2026 hardware survey or bounded freshness search is supplied. Consequently, the materials do not establish whether a classically intractable molecular calculation meeting the proposed accuracy and proof requirements had been demonstrated by the review’s reference date of 2026-11-01. They also do not establish that no such demonstration exists. Both cited sources have empty artifact arrays, limiting verification of their contents and precise scientific scope; those access limitations are missing evidence, not evidence that the reported results are false.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed criterion: publish a classical or quantum algorithm for an explicitly specified family of molecular Hamiltonians, together with an explicit polynomial bound on total computational cost and a complete proof of its energy-error guarantee. Define the computational model, input representation, family restrictions, accuracy dependence, and success probability. Include input preparation, quantum state preparation where applicable, repetitions, and certification in the accounting. These are proposed requirements for a convincing demonstration, not established community standards.
completion_criteria.label: Proved energy-error guarantee and polynomial total cost for molecular family

completion_criteria.text: Proposed accuracy target: demonstrate an error of at most 1 kcal/mol on a strongly correlated complex of the FeMoco type and on a sequence of larger members of the specified family, including a case beyond feasible exact diagonalization. The original research calls 1 kcal/mol the usual chemical-accuracy convention, but the supplied review could not verify that description from source text. It is retained here as an explicit proposed tolerance. State whether it applies to a total energy or a chemically relevant energy difference, and whether it covers only the finite-basis Hamiltonian or also basis and other modeling errors.
completion_criteria.label: Errors ≤1 kcal/mol for FeMoco-type complexes and larger family members

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility requirement: provide the Hamiltonians or sufficient inputs to reconstruct them, implementation details, relevant computational resources, measured costs, and the evidence establishing each reported error bound. Independent reproduction should test both the energy guarantee and the practical cost accounting. For cases beyond exact diagonalization, the validation method must remain meaningful without assuming access to an exact reference calculation that is itself infeasible.
completion_criteria.label: Independent reproduction verifies energy guarantees and practical cost accounting

completion_criteria.text: Compare measured costs across the sequence with the proved polynomial bound and disclose practical limits, including prefactors, precision requirements, and hardware demands. Finite runs can demonstrate breadth and practicality; they cannot prove asymptotic polynomial scaling or literal universality. A density-functional benchmark alone, or a quantum circuit for a classically easy molecule alone, would not satisfy this proposal. Solving every local Hamiltonian is unnecessary, but the claimed molecular-family scope must match the proof and demonstrations.
completion_criteria.label: Measured costs versus polynomial bound, with practical limits disclosed

related_concepts.text: MAT-01, Practical polynomial-time algorithms for NP-complete problems, concerns a broader complexity breakthrough. MAT-08 targets structured molecular energy calculations and permits either a classical or quantum method. Overlap would require additional evidence that a solver’s scope and computational model imply the broader capability. The supplied research’s connection through a general fermionic sign-problem solver is conditional, and the exact theorem attributed to Troyer and Wiese remains unverified in the retained record.

Roster-based comparison: MAT-04, Proved polynomial-cost solution of high-dimensional nonlinear PDEs, shares the ambition of overcoming high-dimensional computational difficulty with rigorous cost and error guarantees. Molecular electronic structure has its own Hamiltonian, antisymmetry, representation, and ground-state requirements. A result for either problem would transfer to the other only through a demonstrated formulation or reduction.

Roster-based comparison: MAT-03, A first-principles theory of turbulent transport, and MAT-07, A prescriptive mathematical theory of deep learning, also seek stronger predictive or computational foundations. Turbulent transport concerns different physical dynamics, while a theory of deep learning concerns learning systems. Neither title supplies MAT-08’s required molecular energy guarantee or polynomial-cost algorithm.

Roster-based comparison: MAT-05, Research-scale machine-checked mathematical discovery, could help develop or verify an algorithm and its proof. Proof assistance would be an enabling capability; MAT-08’s substantive achievement would remain the molecular algorithm, its scope, and its energy and cost guarantees.

Roster-based comparison: MAT-06, Classical polynomial-time integer factorization and discrete logarithms, and MAT-09, Classical polynomial-time algorithms for cryptographic lattice problems, target distinct computational problems and explicitly require classical algorithms. MAT-08 permits quantum computation. Efficient molecular energy estimation would not by itself establish either cryptographic capability.

Roster-based comparison: MAT-02, An effective global Langlands correspondence over number fields, concerns a distinct mathematical correspondence and its effective construction. Its general interest in making difficult mathematics computationally usable does not establish a technical implication for molecular electronic structure. All roster entries remain separate concepts.

unresolved_issues: The cited documents lack retained artifacts, so their passages, precise assumptions, and reported historical results remain unverified in this record.
No supplied freshness search establishes whether the target remained open or had a qualifying demonstration by 2026-11-01.
The intended molecular family, its restrictions, and its practical breadth require specification.
The computational model and polynomial dependence on all relevant input, precision, and success-probability parameters remain unspecified.
The proposed 1 kcal/mol tolerance needs a defined energy reference and error budget; its characterization as a usual convention remains unverified.
A concrete, efficient certification procedure for demonstrations beyond feasible exact diagonalization remains to be identified.
The precise scope of the generic sign-problem hardness result and any applicable complexity restrictions on the intended molecular family require source verification.
